notes.meaning: God called Abraham to test his faith after a long season of peaceful living. The word tested here means to prove or try his trust, not to tempt him to do evil. Abraham answered immediately with Here I am, showing he was completely ready to listen and obey.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the use of the name Elohim here as evidence that the story was woven together from different written documents.

notes.meaning: God commanded Abraham to take Isaac, his beloved and only covenant son, to the land of Moriah. There he was to offer him as a burnt offering, a sacrifice that was killed and completely burned on an altar. Every word made the demand heavier, yet God was testing whether Abraham loved the Giver more than the gift.

Abraham got up early the very next morning without arguing or delaying. He chopped the wood himself, saddled his donkey, and set out with Isaac and two servants toward the designated place. His prompt obedience showed that true faith acts right away even when the command is painful and hard to understand.

On the third day of their journey, Abraham looked up and saw the mountain in the distance. During those three agonizing days of travel, Isaac was already as good as dead in his father's heart. This third day pointed forward to Jesus rising from the dead on the third day.

Abraham told his servants to wait with the donkey while he and Isaac went ahead to worship. He told them that both he and the boy would return together, showing his steady confidence in God. He believed that even if he sacrificed Isaac, God had the power to raise the boy back to life to fulfill His covenant promises.

Abraham placed the heavy wood on Isaac's shoulders while he carried the fire and the sacrificial knife himself. Isaac carrying the wood foreshadows Jesus carrying His own wooden cross to the place of execution. Father and son walked together in quiet agreement and trust.

Isaac noticed that an animal was missing and tenderly asked his father where the lamb for the burnt offering was. This innocent question must have pierced Abraham's heart with intense sorrow. Even so, the father responded with gentle patience and loving calm.

Abraham answered that God Himself would provide the lamb for the burnt offering, and they kept walking on together. While Abraham trusted God to intervene, his answer was also a prophecy pointing to the ultimate Lamb of God who takes away sin. True faith rests in the fact that the Lord will always supply what His people need.

When they reached the place, Abraham built the altar, arranged the wood, and bound Isaac upon it. Isaac was a strong young man who could have resisted, yet he willingly surrendered to his father and to God's command. His quiet submission pictured Christ, who willingly laid down His life in obedience.

Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife, ready to slay his son. His obedience was genuine and complete, not an empty show or half-hearted gesture. God accepted the surrender of Abraham's heart and will as if the sacrifice had already taken place.

Just as Abraham raised the knife, the angel of the LORD called out to him urgently from heaven, repeating his name. Abraham immediately halted and answered, Here I am. This divine messenger intervened at the final second with the full authority of God Himself.

The angel commanded Abraham not to harm the boy, declaring that his reverent fear of God was now proven. To fear God means to hold Him in deep awe, trusting and obeying Him above everything else. God never desired human sacrifice, but He wanted Abraham's wholehearted devotion.

Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught in a nearby thicket by its horns, so he offered it as a burnt offering instead of his son. The ram became a substitute, dying in place of the boy who was spared. This event pointed to Jesus Christ, who died on the cross as the substitute for sinners.

Abraham named that place The LORD Will Provide, celebrating how God intervened in his greatest hour of need. His words became a familiar proverb, reminding future generations that God sees their troubles and provides deliverance on His holy mountain. This mountain later became the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, where Israel worshiped the Lord.

The angel of the LORD called down to Abraham from heaven a second time. Having delivered Isaac and accepted the substitute sacrifice, God spoke again to renew His sacred covenant. This heavenly message brought great assurance and lasting peace to the patriarch.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic interpreters point to God's promise given in response to Abraham's obedience as evidence that good deeds earn merit and reward before God.

notes.meaning: God swore by His own name because Abraham had obeyed and had not withheld his only son. Since there is no greater authority in all the universe, the Lord swore by Himself to prove that His promises can never be broken. When believers give what is dearest to them to God, He honors their faith abundantly.

notes.meaning: God promised to multiply Abraham's descendants so they would be countless like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore. He also promised that his offspring would conquer the gates of their enemies, meaning they would triumph over their foes. This pledge looked to Israel's victories and ultimately to Christ's victory over sin and death.

The Lord declared that all nations on the earth would be blessed through Abraham's offspring because he listened to God's voice. This promise pointed ahead to Jesus Christ, the chosen descendant through whom salvation is offered to the whole world. Abraham's obedience became a channel of life-giving grace to all humanity.

Abraham returned to the servants who were waiting for him, and they all traveled back home to Beersheba together. Isaac went back safely with his father after being spared on the altar. Abraham then settled down in Beersheba to enjoy a season of peace after his greatest trial.

Sometime later, word reached Abraham that his sister-in-law Milcah had given birth to sons for his brother Nahor. Even though Abraham lived far away in Canaan, he was glad to hear that his family back in Haran was flourishing. This message was God's way of introducing the family from which Isaac would later receive a bride.

Milcah's oldest son was named Uz, followed by his brother Buz and Kemuel the father of Aram. Uz may have been the founder of the land where Job lived, and Buz may have been the ancestor of Job's friend Elihu. The Bible records these names to show how God was guiding the broader family lines of Abraham.

Nahor's other sons through Milcah were Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel. While little is remembered about most of these brothers, Bethuel is named because of the key role his child would play in redemptive history. God was quietly working through this distant branch of the family to fulfill His promises.

Bethuel became the father of Rebekah, completing the list of eight sons born to Nahor by Milcah. Rebekah is highlighted here because she would grow up to become Isaac's wife and the mother of Jacob. Even before Abraham began looking for a wife for his son, God's providence had already provided one.

Nahor also had four additional sons named Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah through his concubine Reumah. A concubine was a secondary wife who held fewer legal rights than a primary wife. This completes the record of Nahor's twelve sons, showing the growth of Abraham's extended family.
